title: Task-Contracts Autopsy — Mechanisms
note: Paths relative to BASE defined in OVERVIEW.md. decision defaults to adopt/adapt; reject requires a stated reason.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Agent starts writing a spec/plan on an underspecified request and locks in a wrong interpretation before the user can correct it.
mechanisms.mechanism: Cap clarifying questions at 3-5, ask only where the prompt is ambiguous or missing essential context, present each question with lettered options so the user can answer in one line (e.g. '1A, 2C'), and explicitly forbid starting implementation before the questions are answered.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: This is a thinking aid, not a lookup table: it changes what the model asks itself before acting, not what it renders. It is independently corroborated by grill-for-unknowns' material/grounded/answerable bar (SKILL.md:92-118), which is the same idea from an unrelated author — two independent sources converging on 'ask fewer, sharper questions before building' is a stronger signal than either alone.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Prevents building the wrong thing; does not by itself prevent generic-looking output.
failureModes: Turns into an exhaustive questionnaire if the 3-5 cap and 'only if ambiguous' guard are dropped
Lettered-options format can railroad the user into the agent's framing if the options are not genuinely representative
conflicts: Magnus's own house rule 'Beslut, spørg ikke' (CLAUDE.md) — resolve by keeping the cap very small (1-2 for typical site briefs) and only asking when the answer would change scope/architecture, matching the user's own stated exception clause
mechanisms.testMethod: Run the same ambiguous one-line brief through the skill twice; verify it asks <=5 questions once, then proceeds without re-asking already-answered material.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: A short pre-build question gate in the SiteSmith intake step: max 2-3 lettered questions, asked only when the brief is silent on something that changes layout/scope/brand feel; otherwise proceed with a stated default.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Scope creep and no shared definition of 'done' for a build.
mechanisms.mechanism: Of the 9 mandated PRD sections, two carry real weight for scope control: 'Non-Goals (Out of Scope)' forces the agent to state what it will deliberately not build, and 'Success Metrics' forces a concrete definition of done instead of a vague 'make it work'.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Explicit non-goals are a cheap, model-facing constraint (a few lines) rather than a rendering rule, so they fit the 'thinking aid, not a script' side of Fact 1. They also directly counter the showcase 0/8 failure: if 'do not converge on the same layout as the last brief' were ever stated as a non-goal, it would be a textual constraint the model reasons about, not a template.
requiredContext: any prior similar builds to name as an explicit non-goal reference
mechanisms.outputImpact: Reduces scope drift and gives a checkable definition of done; does not itself diversify visual output.
failureModes: Non-goals section left as boilerplate ('N/A') when unused, adding noise
Success metrics stated in engineering terms (uptime, load time) when the actual failure mode is visual sameness, missing the point
conflicts: The full 9-section PRD template this is extracted from — see prd-full-template reject notes in FAILURE-MODES.md
mechanisms.testMethod: Check a completed brief for an explicit Non-Goals line and a Success Metrics line; confirm the build was later checked against both.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: Two required lines in the SiteSmith brief-intake, not a full PRD: 'this build will not look like <named prior site>' and 'done means <concrete visual/behavioral criterion>'.

mechanisms.problemSolved: A human junior developer misreading a spec written by/for senior engineers.
mechanisms.mechanism: Both files instruct the PRD/task-list author to write for a 'junior developer': explicit, unambiguous, jargon-free.
failureModes: Optimizing prose for a human reader who does not exist in an agent-to-agent handoff wastes tokens on explanations the executing model doesn't need
conflicts: Fact 1: the winning 55-line skill is terse and assumes a capable reader, the opposite of 'explain for a junior dev'
mechanisms.decision_reason: No coherent role in a single website-building skill: the audience is always a capable model reading a compact instruction, not a junior human developer reading a spec. Adopting this framing would add explanatory padding that Fact 1 shows is actively counterproductive.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Work happening on the wrong git branch.
mechanisms.mechanism: Task list generation always inserts a hardcoded '0.0 Create feature branch' as the first task, regardless of context, unless the user opts out.
mechanisms.outputImpact: None for SiteSmith's design mechanism; purely a repo-hygiene step.
failureModes: Fires even when no branch is wanted (solo-dev direct-to-branch workflow, exactly Magnus's own house rule), forcing an explicit opt-out every time instead of reading context
conflicts: Magnus's 'Solo-udvikler, intet PR-flow. Arbejd direkte på grenen' (CLAUDE.md)
Fact 1: this is a decision moved into a fixed rule/lookup-table rather than something the model reasons about from context
mechanisms.decision_reason: This is exactly the class of mechanism Fact 1 warns against: a step executed unconditionally from a rule rather than judged from context, adding a required action with no signal it was ever needed. SiteSmith's own project CLAUDE.md already governs git workflow per-repo.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Agent generates a huge, granular task breakdown before the user has agreed with the high-level shape, wasting a large edit if the shape is wrong.
mechanisms.mechanism: Generate only parent tasks first, present them, and literally pause for the user to type 'Go' before generating sub-tasks.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Cheap two-step confirmation before committing to detail; matches the same idea in grill-for-unknowns' 'Ask for confirmation before build' (SKILL.md:61) from an independent source — convergent evidence for an approval gate before the expensive/detailed step, which is a thinking-order change, not new content generation logic.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Avoids wasted detailed planning when the shape is wrong; no direct visual/design impact.
failureModes: Literal string-match on the word 'Go' is brittle outside a chat-turn interface; needs generalizing to 'any clear affirmative' in a non-interactive agent context
conflicts: Long-run/autonomous-agent house rules (Grok autonomy, context-diamond parent-owns-DoD) that say don't stop-and-wait mid-mission unless the action is irreversible or genuinely ambiguous
mechanisms.testMethod: Verify the skill produces a short parent-task list and stops (does not emit sub-tasks) until an explicit go-ahead signal is present in context.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: One gate, not two: show the proposed site structure/sections before writing any code; proceed automatically if the brief already authorized full autonomy, otherwise wait.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Losing track of which sub-steps of a multi-step build are done, especially across a long or resumed session.
mechanisms.mechanism: The task list markdown file is itself the state: each sub-task line flips from `- [ ]` to `- [x]` as it completes, updated after every sub-task rather than batched per parent task.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: A single small state file is cheap; the risk is exactly what sank the old SiteSmith package — state/config sprawling across many files. Kept to one file, this is fine; multiplied across 139 files it becomes the token-bloat side of Fact 1.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Execution reliability across a long build; no design/visual impact.
failureModes: Proliferating into a state file per phase/per world (mirrors the 139-file sprawl that already lost once)
Checkbox state drifting out of sync with actual code state if updates are batched instead of per-step
conflicts: None direct; complements the existing docs/v3/proof/head-to-head WORKFLOW-STATE.json pattern already in this repo
mechanisms.testMethod: Interrupt a build mid-task-list and resume from the file; confirm the resumed session does not redo completed sub-tasks.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: One flat task-state file per build (not per phase/world), checked off per sub-step; never more than one state file for a single site build.

mechanisms.problemSolved: An agent treats all uncertainty the same way (ask a question), when some uncertainty is a fact to look up, some is taste the user can't verbalize, and some is a risk nobody has named yet.
mechanisms.mechanism: Classify every gap between the plan and reality into known-knowns (cite and restate), known-unknowns (ask or default), unknown-knowns (the user would recognize the right answer if shown it, but can't state the criterion up front — resolve via prototypes/contrasting references, not questions), and unknown-unknowns (risks nobody has named — resolve via a blindspot pass over docs/source/tests).
mechanisms.whyItWorks: This is a pure thinking-mechanism: one short table, no external lookup, that changes how the model routes uncertainty. It maps directly onto the showcase 0/8 failure: three unrelated briefs converging on one house style is the signature of an agent that only handles known-unknowns (asks a question, gets a generic answer) and silently defaults on unknown-knowns (visual taste) instead of routing them to prototypes/contrast.
requiredContext: whatever docs/source/tests exist to check known-knowns against
mechanisms.outputImpact: Directly targets house-style convergence by giving the model an explicit 'this is taste, not a fact — show contrasting options' branch instead of silently choosing a default look.
failureModes: Classifying everything as a known-unknown anyway if the taxonomy is stated but not enforced with a concrete routing rule per quadrant
mechanisms.testMethod: Feed three unrelated site briefs; confirm the unknown-knowns branch actually produces 2-3 contrasting visual directions per brief rather than one default per brief.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: A short quadrant table in the SiteSmith intake instructions, with the unknown-knowns row routing explicitly to 'produce 2-3 contrasting layout/style directions, do not silently pick one'.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Agent conflates its internal model of the problem (the plan, the prompt, its assumptions) with the actual codebase/product/constraints, and never notices the gap.
mechanisms.mechanism: Name the two things separately — 'the map' (prompt, plan, assumptions, prior context) vs 'the territory' (real codebase, constraints, docs, user taste, failure modes) — so 'unknowns' has a crisp definition: the gap between them.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: One paragraph, zero lookup tables, purely a naming/framing device that primes the model to check its assumptions against reality before acting — the cheapest possible thinking aid, squarely on the winning side of Fact 1.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Framing only; no direct output change, but underlies every other mechanism in this package.
failureModes: Framing without a concrete follow-up action (the blindspot pass, the grill loop) is just vocabulary with no behavior change
mechanisms.testMethod: Not independently testable; test via the mechanisms that operationalize it (blindspot pass, grill loop).
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: One line in the SiteSmith system framing: 'the brief is the map, the live constraints (brand, existing pages, real content) are the territory — check the gap before designing.'

mechanisms.problemSolved: Agents that grill relentlessly exhaust the user with low-value questions, or ask vague/unanswerable ones ('what does modern mean to you?').
mechanisms.mechanism: Every question must be material (could change architecture/scope/UX), grounded (points to a concrete doc/source uncertainty), and answerable (user can pick, approve a default, or point to a reference) — delivered via a fixed template (question / why it matters / evidence / recommended default). A ~5-question budget per session, a 'fatigue valve' that stops interviewing on short/impatient answers and converts remaining unknowns into one batched assumptions list, and a rule against asking the user to verbalize taste they can only recognize when shown.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: This is the exact anti-pattern fix the package's own CHANGELOG documents as a deliberate 0.1.2 release (`CHANGELOG.md:13-25`) after real user-exhaustion feedback — it is a tested fix for a known agent failure mode, not a speculative addition. It stays on the 'sharpens thinking' side of Fact 1 because the quality bar and exit conditions are judgment criteria the model applies, not a script that picks the answer for it.
requiredContext: the docs/source uncertainty each one points to
mechanisms.outputImpact: Prevents both over-asking (user fatigue, matches Magnus's explicit 'don't keep asking' house rule) and unanswerable taste-questions (which is exactly what produces a generic default when the user gives up and says 'just pick').
failureModes: Budget/fatigue valve is advisory text; without an explicit counter or turn-tracker an agent can still drift past 5 questions unnoticed
conflicts: None — this directly reinforces, rather than conflicts with, Magnus's 'Beslut, spørg ikke' house rule
mechanisms.testMethod: Run a session with a user who gives one-word answers twice in a row; confirm the agent stops asking and presents a single batched assumptions list instead of a third question.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: The question-quality bar (material/grounded/answerable) and the fatigue valve become the SiteSmith intake gate's only question-asking rule, replacing any open-ended 'anything else?' prompting.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Vocabulary drift (the plan says 'Job', the code says 'Project') causing silent misunderstandings, and undocumented hard-to-reverse decisions that confuse future readers.
mechanisms.mechanism: Maintain a lazily-created `CONTEXT.md` glossary of canonical domain terms (with an 'Avoid: <synonym>' field) and offer an ADR only when a decision is hard to reverse, surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off — never for obvious/reversible/mechanical choices.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Cheap when actually lazy (files created 'only when there is something worth recording', `domain-modeling-add-on.md:34`); becomes overhead if applied to every small build. The three-part ADR gate is a good judgment rule (thinking aid), but the file infrastructure itself only pays for its context cost on multi-page or long-lived builds.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Indirect: reduces miscommunication on complex, multi-session builds; no effect on a single landing page.
failureModes: Creating CONTEXT.md/ADR files by default for every SiteSmith build reintroduces exactly the file-sprawl that produced the 139-file, 630k-token losing package
conflicts: Fact 1 directly, if applied unconditionally — file-based durable-artifact infrastructure is the shape of the mechanism that already lost 40-59
mechanisms.testMethod: Run a one-page landing-site build and a multi-page multi-brand build; confirm CONTEXT.md/ADR files are created for neither, one, or the other in proportion to actual complexity, not by default.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: Keep the three-part ADR gate as a judgment rule for the SiteSmith rebuild's own engineering decisions; do not generate CONTEXT.md/ADR files as part of the standard single-site build flow.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Constraints or failure modes nobody has considered yet (unknown unknowns), which no amount of asking the user about known unknowns will surface.
mechanisms.mechanism: Before interviewing, search the relevant docs/source/tests — including documented limits and known failure modes of load-bearing dependencies — for risks that could materially change the plan; output a ranked list of highest-risk unknown unknowns each with why-it-matters/evidence/cheap-resolution/decision-owner, plus a separate 'likely safe assumptions' list.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Directly operationalizes 'investigate-before-asking' from the task brief: it forces evidence-gathering to happen before any question is asked of the user, which is the single clearest match to what the requester's contract asks for. It is bounded ('run when the user is entering an unfamiliar domain... or high-stakes integration', SKILL.md:136), so it does not fire on trivial tasks.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Surfaces real constraints (e.g. a CMS/hosting limit, a font-licensing restriction) before design work starts, rather than discovering them mid-build.
failureModes: Can turn into an unbounded research spiral without the stated trigger condition (unfamiliar domain/high-stakes) limiting when it runs
mechanisms.testMethod: Point the skill at a brief involving an unfamiliar CMS/integration; confirm it surfaces at least one documented limit before asking the user anything.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: A bounded pre-build check: before design, scan any named platform/CMS/library docs for hard constraints (content limits, hosting quirks, licensing), triggered only when the brief names an unfamiliar target.

mechanisms.problemSolved: The user has taste they will recognize when they see it but cannot specify in words up front ('make it modern') — asking them to verbalize it either gets a useless answer or drives the agent to a generic default.
mechanisms.mechanism: Explicitly ban asking the user to verbalize taste they can only recognize when shown; instead build cheap prototypes showing multiple genuinely contrasting directions (not tiny variations), or point to 2-3 in-repo modules plus one external reference and ask which behavior to match, then distill the user's reaction into a rubric that becomes the verification gate for later work.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: This is the mechanism most directly aimed at SiteSmith's own measured failure: three unrelated briefs converged on one house style (showcase 0/8). The prescribed fix — contrasting directions with meaningful difference, not variations on one theme — is exactly the missing step. It stays cheap (a short instruction, not a lookup table of allowed styles), so it is on the winning side of both measured facts at once: it improves the model's thinking without adding a fixed decision table.
requiredContext: any in-repo or reference sites to contrast against
mechanisms.outputImpact: Directly counters house-style convergence — the single highest-value mechanism found across both sources for this project's stated failure.
failureModes: 'Contrasting directions' can become superficial (same layout, different color) if 'meaningful contrast' is not enforced as a check
mechanisms.testMethod: Re-run the three briefs that previously converged (showcase 0/8, per project memory); confirm the intake step proposes 2-3 visually distinct directions per brief before committing to one.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: A required step before layout/style commitment: propose 2-3 contrasting directions (not variations) per brief, and never silently default to one look without user reaction captured as a rubric.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Mid-build, reality contradicts the plan (a library doesn't support the assumed feature, a constraint was missed) and the agent either barrels ahead wrongly or halts on every tiny surprise.
mechanisms.mechanism: Three-way rule: low-risk/local issues get a conservative choice, logged, and continue; architecture/data/security/cost/user-facing changes stop and ask; and when docs contradict the plan, trust the docs/source over the original plan and update the plan.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: A short, three-branch judgment rule — cheap, and it is the model reasoning about risk level rather than a table mapping situations to actions. Matches the requester's 'stop-on-invalidated-assumption' term precisely.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Keeps autonomous builds from silently going wrong on a bad assumption, without introducing constant check-ins.
failureModes: 'Low-risk and local' is a judgment call; without examples an agent may misjudge a user-facing visual change as 'local'
conflicts: None; complements Magnus's 'default to fix, not diagnose' and 'robust systems over one-off fixes' house rules
mechanisms.testMethod: Inject a mid-build contradiction (e.g. a named font isn't actually licensed for web use) and confirm the agent stops for a user-facing change but silently substitutes-and-logs for a low-risk internal one.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: The same three-branch rule applied to SiteSmith builds: silently substitute-and-log for invisible/internal surprises, stop-and-ask for anything that changes the visible design or brand promise.

mechanisms.problemSolved: A reviewer/user receiving a finished build with no record of what was actually decided, assumed, or verified, forcing them to re-derive it by reading the diff.
mechanisms.mechanism: After implementation, produce: what changed and why, which unknowns were resolved, which assumptions remain, docs/source evidence for important behavior, real verification results (not claimed ones), and — for complex work needing pre-merge understanding — a short quiz/checklist where every item is answerable from the report itself.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Cheap summary discipline; the 'every quiz item answerable from the report' rule is a good self-check against padding, but the quiz format itself is formality that only pays off on complex/reviewed work.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Improves handoff clarity; no direct design/visual impact.
failureModes: Producing a formal quiz for a trivial one-page site is pure padding — the opposite of Fact 1's terse-and-effective lesson
conflicts: Magnus's ADHD-reader house format (§5, INSTRUCTIONS.md) — conclusion-first, max 5 bullets — is a better fit for the summary half of this than a formal quiz
mechanisms.testMethod: Check that a completed build's report states verification results with actual command output/screenshots, not just an assertion that things work.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: Keep the summary (what changed, what's assumed, what was verified) as the standard SiteSmith build report; drop the formal quiz format entirely — it does not match this project's own preferred output shape.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Spawning a subagent or long-running coding agent with an underspecified prompt, so it re-derives context badly or misses the taste/constraint work already done.
mechanisms.mechanism: Before spawning, assemble a launch packet (goal, map, territory to inspect first, the four unknowns categories, deviation policy, verification gates) and, when using multiple subagents, split roles: docs scout, codebase scout, prototype scout (cheap visual/API alternatives specifically to expose unknown-knowns), implementer, reviewer.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: The prototype-scout role is the fan-out equivalent of the unknown-knowns mechanism above — it is the same insight (extract taste via contrast, not questions) applied to a multi-agent architecture. This is directly relevant to how SiteSmith could fan out a build across parallel workers without losing the taste-extraction step in the split.
requiredContext: goal, current plan/prototype, docs/source paths, known/unknown ledgers
mechanisms.outputImpact: Improves subagent output quality by giving each spawned worker only what it needs (thin, role-scoped packets) instead of the full session transcript.
failureModes: Five distinct roles for every build is overkill for a single landing page; the role split only earns its cost on genuinely parallel, multi-surface builds
conflicts: context-diamond skill's own fan-out procedure (already in this user's toolset) — the two should be reconciled rather than run side by side, since context-diamond is the canonical fan-out mechanism this user already standardized on
mechanisms.testMethod: Spawn a prototype-scout-equivalent worker with only its launch packet (no full transcript) and confirm it independently produces contrasting directions without re-asking questions already resolved.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: Fold the prototype-scout role concept into SiteSmith's existing context-diamond fan-out (do not add a second, competing fan-out protocol); keep the launch-packet fields as the minimum context a spawned worker needs.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Two opposite planning failures: an over-specified plan makes the agent follow instructions even when a pivot is obviously better; an under-specified plan makes the agent default to generic best practices that don't fit the actual product.
mechanisms.mechanism: One short paragraph naming both failure directions and their fix: define goal/constraints/stop-continue rules but leave room for implementation judgment (against over-specifying); provide references/docs/taste-examples/acceptance-criteria (against under-specifying).
mechanisms.whyItWorks: This single paragraph is a near-exact post-hoc explanation of both of SiteSmith's own measured failures at once: under-constraining (no taste examples/acceptance criteria) plausibly produced the house-style convergence, while over-constraining (a 139-file, 630k-token package of rules) plausibly produced the loss to a 55-line skill that left room for judgment. Extremely cheap (4 lines), extremely high signal.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Meta-level: a governing principle for how detailed every other SiteSmith instruction should be, not a mechanism with its own output.
failureModes: As a one-paragraph principle it doesn't self-enforce; needs a concrete review step (e.g. 'does this instruction leave a judgment call or does it dictate the answer?') to actually bite
conflicts: None; it is the resolving principle for the tension the task brief itself poses between the two measured facts
mechanisms.testMethod: Not independently testable as a mechanism; test by auditing whether new SiteSmith instructions each state a constraint+goal or instead dictate a specific rendered answer.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: State this calibration paragraph near the top of the rebuilt SiteSmith skill as an explicit editorial principle for every future addition to the skill file.

mechanisms.problemSolved: A skill that silently depends on other skills being installed gives almost nothing to an agent that only loads the headline file.
mechanisms.mechanism: The package's own changelog-of-reasoning: `grill-with-docs` (upstream) was a thin composition skill that depended on two other skills being installed separately; `grill-for-unknowns` inlines the grilling loop and the domain-modeling rules so the whole behavior ships in one self-contained file.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: This is a packaging lesson, not a runtime mechanism, but it is direct, first-party evidence for the same principle this rebuild is already committed to: 'rebuilding SiteSmith as ONE unified skill' (task brief). An unrelated author independently reached the same conclusion after shipping the fragmented version first and finding it didn't work.
mechanisms.outputImpact: Determines whether the rebuilt skill actually works when only its own file is loaded — directly load-bearing for the 'one unified skill' goal.
failureModes: A single file that then re-introduces fragmentation by requiring several external reference files to be read 'first' for basic behavior recreates the same failure under a different file layout
conflicts: None; this is corroborating evidence for the rebuild's own stated architecture
mechanisms.testMethod: Load only the top-level SiteSmith SKILL.md with no reference files present and confirm the described core behavior (question-quality bar, deviation policy, calibration principle) is still present, not just referenced.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: Keep the core loop (question bar, unknowns routing, deviation policy, calibration principle) inline in the single SiteSmith SKILL.md; use reference files only for material genuinely out of the hot path (e.g. detailed ADR formatting).
